interaction_type.value: crack initiation / second crack formation at phase interface

qualitative_or_quantitative_description.value: During tensile tests dislocation accumulation at the interfaces of δ-ferrite band and tempered martensite lamellar, together with the hardness difference between the two phases, promoted stress concentration at their interfaces to induce crack initiation; the crack was captured by δ-ferrite and propagated into and along the δ-ferrite band forming second cracks (deep valleys). The crack propagating into the soft δ-ferrite could be blunted, producing high resistance to cracking, and strain-induced martensitic transformation caused volume expansion promoting crack closure. Second cracks were observed at the interface between δ and γ/α.

interface_notes.value: Sufficient high-angle grain boundaries of coarse δ-ferrite were deficient and could not effectively hinder microcrack propagation, so cleavage morphology formed in δ-ferrite ({100} cleavage is the natural BCC failure mode).

phase_evolution.value: During annealing, reverted austenite nucleated and grew at martensite lath gaps with diffusion of C and Mn into austenite grains and Al into martensite/ferrite; with increasing annealing temperature block boundaries were progressively replaced by austenitic grain (AG) boundaries. For QA-800, small austenite grains grew up and C, Mn in austenite were diluted, raising the Ms temperature so that part of the extremely unstable austenite underwent martensitic transformation in advance during air cooling of annealing.

slip_behavior.value: Dislocation gliding started sequentially in ferrite and austenite as well as tempered martensite according to the difference of phase hardness; decreasing GND density in the annealed tempered martensite and austenite made dislocation slip easier, lowering yield strength.

unmapped_findings: QA-800: yield-tensile ratio 0.65 (lowest among QA specimens) and product of strength and elongation (PSE) 36.2 ± 2.9 GPa% (Table 3).
QA-800 austenite volume fraction by EBSD ~49 % and by XRD ~48 % (Table 2).

The austenitic stability constant k of QA-800 is ~1.50 (second highest among QA specimens), indicating relatively low austenitic stability and a notable TRIP effect; SFE ~31.53 mJ·m^-2 which lies between 20 and 40 mJ·m^-2, so TWIP effect was supposed to exist during deformation.

For QA-800, newly formed martensite during air cooling of the annealing treatment deteriorated ductility; less austenite experienced the TRIP effect than in QA-740, giving a relatively lower total elongation (50.4 %) than QA-740 (62.4 %).

QA-800 block boundary density decreased and AG boundary density instead decreased at 800 °C (due to some coarse austenite grains); the lowest block-boundary and GND densities contributed to the lowest yield strength among QA specimens.

Grain boundary classification used in the study: 5°–15°, 15°–45°, and >45°; high-angle boundaries (>15°) are regarded as critical to mechanical properties; AG boundaries (15°–45°) and block boundaries (>45°) were the two highest boundary densities; a Python machine-learning model (Li et al.) was used to identify boundary types and calculate boundary density.

The steel after QA treatment (including QA-800) exhibited a wide yield strength grade range of 460–620 MPa with excellent ductility (40–63 %) and low yield-tensile ratio (0.65–0.75), being a typical third-generation advanced high-strength steel.
